subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: follow-up check-ins and adjusting the arrangement [Revision]
passage: Two weeks after the new handover rules began, Avni booked ten minutes with each of the two in the glass meeting room. Sonali went first. "The rules help, but the note takes me forty minutes and nobody reads to the end." Then Vishal said the same thing in different words: too long. Avni looked at the template on the screen. It had nine headings. Together they cut it down to three: changed, pending, contact. Both nodded. "I'll ask again next month," Avni said, and put a fifteen-minute slot in the calendar for the first Friday of each month. Sonali left the room looking lighter, and Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

qa.q: How many headings did the template have?
How did Sonali feel on leaving the meeting room?
qa.a: Sonali felt lighter and relieved, since the note would no longer take forty minutes.

qa.q: What else could Avni do at the monthly check-in, and why?
qa.a: Avni could ask whether anyone reads the shortened notes and change the format again if not, because a rule should be adjusted until it serves the people using it.

qa.q: How might Vishal have seen the two-week check-in?
qa.a: Vishal probably felt listened to and glad the complaint led to a quick change, since Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

grounding: Illustrates a lead checking after two weeks how new working rules are going, shortening a too-long handover note and keeping a short monthly check-in.
